You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power sensor-node $R_L$ from storage $C_{out}$ at node "out".
    *   Requirements:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$. $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (nominal).

    *   `sshi_fbr_zener` (topology 40eae91a637a):
        *   Structure: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) + FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) + Zener clamp.
        *   Results: Passed 5/6. S3 failed on ripple (62 mV vs 50 mV).
        *   S3 is strong excitation (100 uA), light load (2200 kOhm).
        *   S3 ripple is caused by the pulsed nature of the SSHI charge delivery into $C_{out}$. Since the load is very light, $V_{out}$ rises, and the Zener clamps it. The ripple is $V_{pp}$.
        *   Wait, the ripple is $v_{pp} = 62\text{ mV}$. The Zener is `DZ33` (3.3V). The average voltage on S3 is 3.39 V. This means the Zener is conducting and limiting the voltage.
        *   Actually, look at the results for S3: $v_{avg} = 3.39\text{ V}$, $v_{max} = 3.41\text{ V}$, $v_{pp} = 62\text{ mV}$. The ripple is high.

    *   The ripple in SSHI is caused by the periodic delivery of energy from the inductor $L$ into $C_{out}$ via the rectifier diodes.
    *   The current pulses from the inductor are large and short ($\sim \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$).
    *   To reduce ripple, we need:
        1.  Larger $C_{out}$.
        2.  Smoother current delivery.
        3.  Lower source current (not possible, S3 is a fixed condition).
    *   In `sshi_fbr_zener`, $C_1$ was $9.25\text{ }\mu\text{F}$. Wait, the log says $9.25\text{e-07}$ F (0.925 uF).
    *   Wait, the reference design FBR used $2.2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and had $v_{pp} = 26.2\text{ mV}$ (S1). $0.925\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ is smaller, which explains the higher ripple.
    *   However, if $C_{out}$ is too large, $t_{up}$ might exceed 0.4 s or $dv$ might exceed 0.02 V.
    *   Wait, if the only failure is S3 ripple (62 mV), and S3 has the *lightest* load (2.2 MOhm), why is the ripple higher than S1 (36 mV) or S2 (44 mV)?
    *   In S3, the excitation $I_p$ is $100\text{ }\mu\text{A}$ (double the nominal). The energy delivered per pulse is much larger.
    *   $C_{out}$ needs to be larger to dampen the larger pulses of S3, but not so large that $t_{up}$ or $dv$ fail.

    *   The current `sshi_fbr_zener` is:
        *   L1: pzp to n1
        *   S1: n1 to pzn
        *   D1: pzp to out
        *   D2: pzn to out
        *   D3: 0 to pzp
        *   D4: 0 to pzn
        *   D5: 0 to out (DZ33)
        *   C1: out to 0
    *   Wait, is this a standard FBR? A full bridge usually has 4 diodes.
        *   D1: pzp -> out
        *   D2: pzn -> out
        *   D3: 0 -> pzp
        *   D4: 0 -> pzn
        *   This is not a standard bridge. A standard bridge is:
            *   D1: pzp -> out
            *   D2: pzn -> out
            *   D3: 0 -> pzp (Wait, the anode is 0, cathode is pzp)
            *   D4: 0 -> pzn (Anode 0, cathode pzn)
            *   Let's check current flow:
                *   When $V_{pzp} > 0$, $D1$ conducts (pzp to out), $D4$ conducts (0 to pzn). Current: $0 \to pzn \to \text{piezo} \to pzp \to out \to 0$. (Correct)
                *   When $V_{pzp} < 0$, $D2$ conducts (pzn to out), $D3$ conducts (0 to pzp). Current: $0 \to pzp \to \text{piezo} \to pzn \to out \to 0$. (Correct)
            *   Yes, it is a full bridge.
    *   The problem is the ripple on S3. To fix this, we might need a larger $C_{out}$. But the tuner already tried to optimize $C_1$ (it reached $0.925\text{ }\mu\text{F}$).
    *   Is there a way to reduce the current spikes?
    *   Adding a small series resistor or inductor between the rectifier and $C_{out}$ could smooth the current, but the rectifier is already connected to "out".
    *   Alternatively, can we use a different topology?
    *   Maybe a "half-bridge" or a "voltage doubler"? No, the goal is to maintain 1.8V-3.6V. SSHI is usually the most efficient.
    *   Let's look at the SSHI part. The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ invert the voltage across $C_p$.
    *   Another option: Use a different storage arrangement. Instead of a single $C_{out}$, maybe use an LC filter? But that adds components.
    *   Wait, the ripple is only 62 mV vs 50 mV. This is very close. Maybe the tuner just didn't find the sweet spot for $C_{out}$ because of the $dv$ or $t_{up}$ constraints?
    *   Wait, $dv$ is the change in mean voltage between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s. A larger $C_{out}$ *decreases* $dv$ (it's more stable), but *increases* $t_{up}$ (takes longer to charge).
    *   Let's re-evaluate the current topology. The SSHI-FBR is very strong. The only issue is S3 ripple.
    *   Is there a way to reduce the peak current?
    *   If we add a small inductor in series with the rectifier output? No, that would create a second-order circuit and potentially more ripple.
    *   What if we use a different diode model? `DSCH` is already the lowest drop.
    *   What if we use a different Zener? `DZ33` is already used.

    *   `sshi_fbr_zener` used 10 components. We have 16.
    *   Could we use a "Parallel-SSHI" or something to split the current?
    *   Actually, the simplest way to reduce ripple in a pulsed system is to increase the capacitance. But the tuner already tried to optimize it. Let's look at the limits: $C_{max} = 4.7\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.
    *   If $C_{out}$ was $4.7\text{ }\mu\text{F}$, would $t_{up}$ fail?
    *   $t_{up}$ for S4 (weakest) was $0.2\text{ s}$ with $C_1 = 0.925\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.
    *   If $C_1$ increases to $4.7\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ (a factor of 5), $t_{up}$ might increase to $\sim 1\text{ s}$. That would fail (limit is 0.4 s).
    *   So we are in a trade-off: $C_{out}$ must be large enough to keep S3 ripple $< 50\text{ mV}$ but small enough to keep S4 $t_{up} < 0.4\text{ s}$.

    *   The ripple is caused by the current pulses from the inductor.
    *   $I_{peak} \approx V_{pzp} / \sqrt{L/C_p}$.
    *   To reduce $I_{peak}$ while keeping the same energy transfer, we need a larger $L$.
    *   Wait, $L$ was $0.01\text{ H}$. Max $L$ is $0.01\text{ H}$. It's already at the max.
    *   Wait, if we increase $L$, the peak current $I_{peak}$ decreases and the pulse width $\Delta t$ increases.
    *   $Q_{pulse} = \int I dt$. The charge delivered per pulse is roughly the same.
    *   $\Delta V \approx Q_{pulse} / C_{out}$.
    *   Actually, the ripple $\Delta V$ depends primarily on $Q_{pulse}$ and $C_{out}$, not on the shape of the pulse (as long as the pulse is much shorter than the period).
    *   $Q_{pulse} \approx 2 C_p V_{pzp}$.
    *   So $\Delta V \approx 2 C_p V_{pzp} / C_{out}$.
    *   For S3: $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $V_{pzp} \approx 3.3\text{ V}$, $C_{out} = 0.925\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.
    *   $\Delta V \approx (2 \cdot 25\text{e-9} \cdot 3.3) / 0.925\text{e-6} \approx 165\text{e-9} / 0.925\text{e-6} \approx 0.178\text{ V} = 178\text{ mV}$.
    *   Wait, the measured ripple was 62 mV. This is because the ripple is the *peak-to-peak* of the output voltage, and the pulses are averaged over the period.
    *   Actually, $v_{pp}$ is the peak-to-peak ripple of $V_{out}(t)$.
    *   The load $R_L$ (2.2 MOhm for S3) is very large, so the discharge between pulses is minimal.
    *   The ripple is almost entirely the "sawtooth" created by the charge pulses.
    *   $V_{pp} \approx Q_{pulse} / C_{out}$.
    *   To reduce $V_{pp}$, we *must* increase $C_{out}$. But $C_{out}$ is limited by $t_{up}$.

    *   Can we deliver charge more continuously?
    *   The current SSHI-FBR delivers charge in two pulses per period (one at each peak).
    *   What if we use a different SSHI configuration?
    *   Or a "Charge Pump" approach?
    *   What if we add a second storage capacitor and alternate between them? (A "ping-pong" capacitor approach).
    *   Wait, the components limit is 16.
    *   Let's try to implement a simple charge-smoothing circuit.
    *   If we put a small inductor in series with the rectifier? No, that's just an LC filter, which might oscillate or increase $t_{up}$.
    *   Wait, what if we use a different rectification method?
    *   The current bridge is:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
    *   This is a standard full bridge.

    *   $C_{out}$ is too small for S3 ripple, but too large for S4 $t_{up}$.
    *   We need to deliver charge more effectively during start-up (to allow a larger $C_{out}$) or deliver charge more smoothly (to allow a smaller $C_{out}$).
    *   To deliver charge more effectively during start-up:
        *   The current system is SSHI. SSHI is very efficient.
        *   Maybe the Zener clamp is hindering start-up? No, Zener only conducts above 3.3V.
        *   Maybe the diode drops are the problem? `DSCH` is already used.
    *   Let's consider the "Symmetric SSHI" or other variants.
    *   Actually, there's a simpler way to reduce ripple: a larger $C_{out}$.
    *   Let's check if $C_{out} = 2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ would pass $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ on S4.
    *   In the reference FBR, $C_{out} = 2.2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and $t_{up}$ on S4 was "FAIL" (missing).
    *   But SSHI delivers much more power than FBR.
    *   In `sshi_fbr_zener`, $C_{out} = 0.925\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and $t_{up} = 0.2\text{ s}$.
    *   If we double $C_{out}$ to $1.85\text{ }\mu\text{F}$, $t_{up}$ should roughly double to $0.4\text{ s}$.
    *   And the ripple on S3 should halve from 62 mV to 31 mV.
    *   This would solve S3 ripple and just barely pass S4 $t_{up}$.
    *   But the tuner already explored the value space. Why didn't it find $C_{out} \approx 1.8\text{ }\mu\text{F}$?
    *   Maybe because of $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$?
    *   $dv = |mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)|$.
    *   For S3, $R_L$ is 2.2 MOhm. The power delivered is $P_{in}$.
    *   If $P_{in} > P_{load}$, $V_{out}$ will rise until the Zener clamps it.
    *   Once clamped at 3.3V, the mean voltage is constant, so $dv$ will be very small.
    *   Wait, if the Zener is clamping, $dv$ should be fine.
    *   So why did the tuner stop at $0.925\text{ }\mu\text{F}$?
    *   Perhaps because $V_{out}$ was still rising?
    *   Let's look at the S3 results for `sshi_fbr_zener`: $v_{avg} = 3.39\text{ V}$, $v_{max} = 3.41\text{ V}$.
    *   The Zener `DZ33` is not a perfect clamp; it has a slope.
    *   $V_{avg} = 3.39\text{ V}$ means the Zener is conducting.
    *   The ripple $v_{pp} = 62\text{ mV}$ is the problem.

    *   If I can't change the topology to something fundamentally different, maybe I can try to optimize the existing one by suggesting a different value for $C_{out}$? No, the tuner does that.
    *   Wait, I can't just suggest values. I must suggest a *topology*.
